tried) nor globally for all aroma.affymetrix actions.  One redesign

object which in turn defaults to a global verbose.  However, this far
this is just thoughts.

messages.subject: Re: missing C function from affyPLM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ken and all,

So I have looked at Henrik's code for getFitFunction.RmaPlm. It has
changed substantially, and in particular, it has catches for
evaluating what is the version of affyPLM being used, and the newer
version calls from the 'preprocessCore' package. I wonder if it would
not be possible to use the 'RmaPlm' version of getFitFunction for the
exon array -- the main difference is calling median polish if there
are too many probesets per transcript cluster, right? Henrik has
different 'flavors' in getFitFunction.RmaPlm function (e.g. oglio) and
we could make an 'manyProbesets' flavor that would do a check on the
dimensions and then pick median polish or IWLS one? Or somehow make
Henrik's code about choosing the fitting function more modular so that
getFitFunction.ExonRmaPlm can grab ahold of it? It just seems
pointless (and against the point of object oriented programming!) to
copy all the work Henrik does in keeping the getFitFunction up-to-
date. And clearly a recipe for disaster for mantaining the package.

I don't remember how much impact these two approaches would have (i.e.
how trickle down to other functions). What's your take on this, Ken?
(and Henrik, of course, when you get back, since either way requires a
change to your core code) Is it better to 1) make a 'flavor' within
getFitFunction.RmaPlm for the exon array fitting function and get rid
of getFitFunction.ExonRmaPlm altogether or 2) cut out some of the
functions defined in getFitFunction.RmaPlm (e.g.
'getRlmPkg','rmaModelAffyPlmOld','rmaModelAffyPlm', etc.) and make
them globally available to be called appropriately (based on
dimension) by getFitFunction.ExonRmaPlm?  or 3) Both! make a large
number of probes 'flavor' (so get rid of ExonRmaPlm method) AND make
the functions more globally available. Henrik's code for the
getFitFunction.RmaPlm has additional advantages, in addition to
defining these functions -- validating that the answers make sense,
etc -- which we might as well not recreate either. Would there be some
interest by users in having the option to do median polish fitting
anyway for speed reasons? Perhaps it might be nice to make those
fitting functions somewhat globally available regardless (at a
developers level, not general users) if there are future uses of them
and then they only have to be mantained once.

In the meantime, I am going to patch in Henrik's code to update
getFitFunction.ExonRmaPlm. When (if?) I get it working, I'll give it
to Henrik to make available as a patch.

Best,
Elizabeth

The 'ram' argument is a scale factor that allows you to adjust if you
want aroma.affymetrix to process data in smaller chunks (raw < 1) or
large chunks (raw > 1) than default (raw = 1).

It's main purpose is to make an algorithm to run in less memory if it
turns out that it is consuming large amount of memory.  Use a process
manager/Unix 'top' and/or detailed verbose output to see the memory
consumption.  If R is consuming more memory than available RAM, it
will start swapping RAM to disk ("virtual memory") and that will slow
down the processing 100-1000 fold!  If this happens set 'ram' to a
smaller value.

Other than avoiding swapping, the value of 'ram' does not affect the
speed very much (unless you set 'ram' to be a ridiculously small value
so that say only a few probesets are processed in every chunk, because
then the relative IO overhead will dominate).

>     plotNuse(qam)

Yes, setting up the output device before calling a plot function in R
is better.  It will generate better looking graphs because R optimizes
the layout to the target device.  When using dev.print(), R cannot do
this.

However, the time to generate the plot will be roughly the same.

The QualityAssementModel class, which plotNuse() operates on, was
written some time ago by Ken Simpson.  It has partly been optimized
for speed, but not in full, so maybe some improvements can be done to
the implementation.

However, if you look at the plotNuse.QualityAssementModel function
(please do that), you'll see that there several intermediate steps
done and some of these takes time.  Some of the methods
(automagically) cache their results to file so that when calling them
the next time will be much faster.

Again, use the 'verbose' argument to track down what takes time - it
often makes sense we you see it.

Moreover, to calculate an approximate NUSE, you can specify the
fraction of data, in (0,1], to be used by using argument 'subset'.
That way not all data has to be loaded and you will still get
reasonable results.

Example:

verbose <- Verbose(threshold=-30);
timestampOn(verbose);
...
plotNuse(qam, subset=1/3, verbose=verbose);

to track down what takes time.

/Henrik

Hi Ju,

Following up on Henrik's helpful references to the other discussions...

I looked at the Affy's cdf (that I also got from Ken) where each unit is
just a probeset. Is that the one you are using Ju?

As described in one of the posts Henrik referenced, there are a number
of Affy defined probesets that have more than 4 probes. According to
their documentation, this should not happen (except maybe non aligned
mRNA probesets?), so I think these are due to quality control probes or
an error in their cdf file. Another oddity: unlike all of the other
units which are just a single probeset, there is one unit that has
(many) groups with variable number of probes per group -- one group has
31259 probes, but even the other groups have 75-300. Again, these are
clearly some kind of controls -- they also could be the genomic
background controls that we were told were combined into one probeset.

A summary of these probesets (not including the 'oddity') -- note some
very large numbers of probes even then!
 > summary(unlist(nprobesPerUnit[whichBig[whichBig!=hasGroups]]))
    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
    5.00    40.25    91.00   367.50    96.75 16890.00

Anyway, since you are fitting probeset by probeset, I think you should
remove any probeset that has more than 4 probes, at least for the model
fitting stage. While the controls might be useful for background control
(although we're not currently using them smartly) they certainly don't
need a linear model fit to them, especially since we don't know what
controls are being thrown together as 1 probeset. If you change and are
fitting by transcript cluster, there will still be transcript clusters
with large numbers of probes. But you can't get around that -- those are
biologically relevant!

Another interesting note is that the cdf Ken created for 'full' has some
of these probesets with more than 4 probes per probeset. But they only
have 20-40 probes per probeset, so the really huge ones have been cut
out. So if you used that cdf and then use mergeGroups=FALSE, you would
have a probeset by probeset fitting without the really huge ones. I
don't know what these probesets are -- i.e. if they are legit; they may
be mRNA products that do not align to the genome. A big think on my
to-do list is to go back to these cdf definitions and try to both update
them according to Affy's new annotation and to check out these strange
probesets and create a quality control cdf.

Ju, could you tell us how long it takes when you remove these unit
(assuming you're using that cdf)?

nprobesPerUnit<-readCdfNbrOfCellsPerUnitGroup(getPathname(cdf),unit=NULL)
whichBig<-which(sapply(nprobesPerUnit,function(x){any(unlist(x)>4)}))
fit(plm,units=indexOf(cdf,names=names(nprobesPerUnit[-whichBig])),...)

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] changes to FirmaModel class
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,
You can do the same basic strategy (of course overwriting what's
already there) -- it's just harder to get the definitions of the class
objects. I do this in a round about way by debugging 'FirmaModel'
because it prints out the class function and then 'args' to see the
function call, but there must be a better way to see the code of
functions that are not available. Anyway, doing this, I reconstruct
that the call for FirmaModel is as below. You can see that the only
error catching is that 'summaryMethod' must be a string, so you can
add new options to getUnitFitFunction.FirmaModel, or whatever it is,
and it won't matter. I would note that the default 'tag' is FIRMA, but
you might want a different tag for different summary methods. In
addition, back in the spring, at least, the names of the files that
the scores were saved to were hard coded in the fit function, not
according to the tags (I think), and so I don't know how well the tags
go through the process.

Best,
Elizabeth

setConstructorS3("FirmaModel",function (rmaPlm = NULL, summaryMethod =
"upperQuartile", tags = "*", ...) {
    if (!is.null(tags)) {
        tags <- Arguments$getCharacters(tags)
        tags <- trim(unlist(strsplit(tags, split = ",")))
        asteriskTag <- "FIRMA"
        tags[tags == "*"] <- asteriskTag
        tags <- paste(tags, collapse = ",")
        tags <- unlist(strsplit(tags, split = ","))
    }
    if (!is.character(summaryMethod)) {
        throw("Argument 'summaryMethod' must be a string.")
    }
    extend(UnitModel(..., tags = tags), "FirmaModel", .plm = rmaPlm,
        summaryMethod = summaryMethod, "cached:.fs" = NULL)
})

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

you may also extend the FirmaModel class into say, MyFirmaModel class
and play with that.  Then you modifications will not interfere with
the existing implementation. When you're happy with your new
model/mods, then they can be "lifted" up in the superclass, e.g.

setConstructorS3("MyFirmaModel",function (..., tags=c("*", "my", "tags")) {
   extend(FirmaModel(..., tags=tags), "MyFirmaModel",
     .myField1 = "foo",
     .myField2 = "bar"
   )
})

and all methods are inherited.  To override a method in FirmaModel, e.g.

setMethodS3("fit", "MyFirmaModel", unction (...) {
  ...
})

Cheers

Henrik
